en: Regarding the complete ritual procedure for establishing the maṇḍala and performing homa:

on the first day, one should empower oneself with the nature of the Tathāgata, make offerings to and alert the earth deity (pṛthivī-devatā), select the site by removing all harmful substances, and construct it so that it is firm and solid; on the second day, one should excavate a pit within the altar.

At the elbow, empower the five precious substances and so forth with Acala; establish the positions of the deities of the mandala, marking the sites of the five Buddhas and four Bodhisattvas with white sandalwood paste.
On the third day, place the ritual vases and empower them one hundred and eight times with the Acala mantra.
On the evening of the fourth day, next recite the perfume mantra one hundred and eight times and then perform the ritual sprinkling for purification.
On the fifth day, perform the protection of the body and the offering by reciting the mantra of Acala or Trailokyavijaya one hundred and eight times; next, recite the Bhūmiparigraha-vidyā.

On the sixth night, the master and disciples bathe, put on clean robes, and proceed to the maṇḍala to perform offerings according to the ritual; with hands joined in the appropriate mudrā, they press upon the central womb [of the maṇḍala], reciting the vidyā once for each press up to seven times, following the same procedure for the positions of all the deities.
On the seventh day, the master next instructs the disciples in the three refuges, repentance, and the generation of the bodhicitta.
I bow my head and take refuge, paying homage to all the Bhagavāns,
as well as the Dharma and all the Bodhisattvas,
and to Guhyakapada, the Great Wrathful One!
To benefit others, one should practice yoga to swiftly achieve great siddhi;
remaining free from all faults, one establishes the maṇḍala and sets forth the homa ritual.
First, by means of the pure dharma-realm, one establishes the receptacle world; then,
contemplating the wondrous bodhicitta, one’s body becomes identical to a sattva,
its color like that of emerald crystal, abiding within the karma-cakra.
With the Great Mantra King, one pervades all parts of the body:
the syllable “Aṃ” is at the crown; “Khaṃ Aṃ” is on the left and right ears;
that which is on the forehead is named “Aḥ”; and “Saṃ So” is on the two shoulders.
"HAM HA" constitutes the throat and heart; "RAM HA" forms the navel and waist;
"VAM VA" constitutes the thighs and feet.
At these three locations, the disciple’s mandala is consecrated according to the rite, becoming everywhere a mass of flaming garlands.
When one encounters an auspicious day, time, and hour, with the lunar mansions and planets all in harmony,
and before the meal, amidst signs of good fortune, one should select the ground and remove all faults and evils.
First, pay homage to all Tathāgatas!
Awaken the Earth Deities!
One should recite these verses as follows:
The Sanskrit is like a womb;
you, Devaśarman, its protector, have practiced sublime conduct toward the Buddhas,
the Teachers, and have purified the stages and the perfections.
Just as the Lion of the Śākyas, the Savior of the World, destroyed the hosts of Māra,
so too shall I subdue Māra. As I draw the maṇḍala,
kneeling long with my right hand extended, I press upon the earth and repeatedly recite this verse.
With fragrant ointments, flowers, and the like, one should make offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and the retinues of the Earth Goddess!
Sprinkling pure scented water and further preparing the ground, the Earth Goddess maintains the proper sequence.
The mantra is as follows:
With the vajra-bind, open the palms; practice pressing them upward twenty-one times, and likewise for pressing downward; thus one immediately accomplishes the Firm Earth.
Having swept, sprinkled, and wiped [the site], seven days prior to the ceremony, at dusk,
one should take incense and flowers and enter alone to the place where the altar is to be set.
Facing east and holding an incense burner, recite the verse for requesting the earth:
“May all Buddhas who have compassion for sentient beings, Please turn their mindful attention toward us.
I now address these worthy sages: The Earth Goddess Sthāvarā and her retinue, All Tathāgatas and the sons of the Buddha!”

Without forsaking your compassionate vows, descend upon me all together; I offer this place for the sake of attaining accomplishment—act as my witnesses and grant me your protection, [recite] three times.
Having made this earnest invitation, the assembly of sages gathers like clouds;
the pure body of Vairocana pervades the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so.
With the utmost sincerity of the three karmas, I pay homage.
Kneeling with both knees on the ground, firmly hold the vajra at the heart,
keeping it straight and upright; extend the fingers of the wisdom hand into five spokes and place the palms flat upon the earth, as previously done when alerting the Earth Deity.
Each time after reciting and each time after pressing [the seal], one should practice the root mantra one hundred and eight times,
and with utmost sincerity, address this petition:
"I reverently entreat all Tathāgatas!"
To the assembly of great Bodhisattvas, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, and to the spirits and deities of this place: I, [Name],
announce my request for whatever matters I seek, in accordance with the teachings of the Vidyādharapiṭaka.
Holding the mantra of such-and-such a deity, for the sake of seeking the Unsurpassed Way,
I wish to establish a maṇḍala within this place and diligently practice recitation;
I pray that the Honored One will remember your original vow.
Grant me this establishment; protect and assist me so that the celestial Māras, evil spirits, and ghosts do not cause affliction, confusion, or obstacles.
When Śākyamuni sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued the hosts of Māra and his enemies.
I am likewise so now.
Should there be any obstacles or difficulties, I pray that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will not allow demons or spirits to falsely manifest deceptive delusions.
If there are no obstacles or hindrances, may you behold the auspicious state.
Sitting in silent composure, recite the fundamental mantra and vidyā one thousand and one hundred times or more, remaining free from all discursive thoughts.
Having completed the recitation, one sleeps peacefully, focusing the mind on the bodhicitta;
within the moon-disc maṇi jewel, both the accomplished and the unaccomplished appear with extreme clarity,
inside and out, all reflected in the mirror of the mind.
One who acts with unwholesome force may fear bringing about self-injury.
First, having properly established the preliminary signs, place the site in the center;
each side of the square measures one cubit, and one should dig it out, removing tiles and stones.
Then fill it in until level and even, examining its solidity and emptiness.
If it is fit for construction, stabilize it with the *mudrā* of the Mother and protect the ground one hundred and eight times; thereafter, one should dig it out entirely.
Form the mudrā of the spade by binding the vajra-fist; extend the thumbs, the wisdom fingers, and the index fingers.
The mantra is as follows (21):
"Discard all impurities and evils that are unfit to replace [the soil] in the Pure Land."
Repeatedly sprinkle scented water until it is as level and real as a clear mirror.
Upon the heart-mandala place the five treasures, namely:
gold, silver, pearl, musāragalva, and crystal.
The "efficacious medicines" refer to:
ginseng and *fuling* (poria), calamus, *tianmendong* (asparagus),
rice grains, large and small wheat, mung beans, sesame, and so forth.
Sandalwood, agarwood, clove, saffron, and *nāgakesara* incense,
placed in vessels of gold or silver, are consecrated one hundred and eight times by the Earth Goddess (*Pṛthivīdevatā*).
These are mixed with perfumed water and empowered by Aparājita or Hayagrīva.

The mantra for smearing the ground is: *Oṃ kārale mahākārale svāhā*. One should smear and wipe from the northeast corner, circling to the right, using a mixture of lotus seeds, hibiscus leaves, *agaru* (eaglewood), and black earth. Rub and polish it according to the ritual rules until it is bright and clean.

The mantra for sweeping the ground is: *Oṃ hara hara jvālāharaṇaya svāhā*. Once again, sprinkle pure scented water. Apply white sandalwood paste to the honored seat and recite the *karmaprasādhinī* mantra one thousand times.
Next, with eyes of compassion, one contemplates all sentient beings;
having practiced the clarity of the nectar of immortality,
the eight-petaled lotus arises from the mind at the place where the Teacher dwells.
Upon a lotus flower of supreme majesty and beauty, in the midst of a perfectly full lunar disc,
stainless as a pure mirror— therein he dwells eternally,
the Mantra Lord, Savior of the World!
Golden-hued and endowed with radiant flames, having subdued poison and abiding in samādhi, they are as difficult to gaze upon as the sun.
So it is with you, O virtuous ones: within that perfect mirror, you shall see your own physical forms identical to the body of a Buddha.
To perform this visualization, first contemplate external conditions and subsequently draw them into one's own body.
With a topknot of a hundred rays of light, illuminating boundless realms,
one should skillfully regulate the mind and breath while reciting the mantra of the syllable "A" in continuous succession.
For one breath, or even up to three, one should recite with all one's might;
when the sensation of contact accords with the mind, free from all conceptual discrimination,
one establishes the maṇḍala from the essence of the pure dharmadhātu.
I prostrate to the Bhagavān and to Prajñāpāramitā!
Next, having prepared the colors and protected them from harm,
one should arrange the various noble deities.
Then one should paint the adorned body [of the deity] and next arrange it for the homa; this is the subtle and secret method of accomplishment.
One should establish the maṇḍala within a newly purified chamber.
Arranging exquisite incense and flowers, one makes offerings with sincere devotion;
according to the rite, one performs the purification.
Through acts such as magnetizing and subjugating, their majestic spiritual power is unfathomable.
Able to transform the minds of heaven and earth, its efficacy is boundless;
it extensively unfolds the blessings of all sentient beings.
Bestowing grace upon many, it accords with the various aspirations sought by each according to their kind.
Each is distinguished individually.
Homa is briefly of two kinds, namely, internal and external.
Regarding internal homa:
Since all those sentient beings are born from karma, one who purifies karma attains liberation;
that which can incinerate past karma is what is called the bodhicitta.
This is called internal homa.
While ordinary homa burns substances into ashes, this is not so;
for the sake of one's own fierce and sharp wisdom, it burns away all afflictions.
Like the fire at the end of an eon that leaves no embers behind, the three places are of one single essence: the great maṇḍala is itself the homa;
the homa is one's own body.
One's own body is the Fire Deity;
the Fire Deity is Mahāvairocana.
These three are equal and without distinction, fully endowed with the three bodies (trikāya).
Its measure pervades the entire Dharma-realm; it neither arises nor ceases.
It is beyond words and beyond the characteristics of words; whether as arising or as non-arising, there is nothing that is not the Venerable Mahāvairocana!
Shrouded by the obscurations of delusion, one enters into fierce wisdom;
blazing all around like a raging fire at the end of an eon,
it holds swords and nooses to incinerate karma and afflictions.
The stumps and stumps of ignorance and so forth shall no longer remain as remnants.
Next, contemplate the bodhicitta; bathe it with the water of great compassion.
One should imagine white nectar flowing and permeating throughout the entire body.
Sprinkled throughout the lands of the ten directions, it nourishes all sentient beings afflicted by heat and torment, causing the sprouts of bodhicitta to grow and giving birth to successive sons.
This is the five-wheeled syllable that constitutes the Buddha-body; this is what is called the Dharma-body, the secret inner homa.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"After I have attained Bodhi, I shall expound twelve kinds [of teachings].
The light of wisdom from the bodhicitta is square in shape and golden-yellow in color."
Surrounded by a wreath of flames, abiding in the samādhi of tranquility, one should visualize while reciting the secret mantra; this can accomplish all matters.
Following the worldly methods for the mandala and hearth, all offerings and garments shall be yellow.
In the second row is Pūrṇāgni; his form resembles the autumn moon, with radiance spreading everywhere. His body and robes are pure white;
he is within a lunar-maṇḍala, holding a jewel and a water flask.
It removes the calamities of water, fire, insects, and frost; it cures the diseases of oneself and others,
as well as all manner of evil misfortunes and the wavering, unstable mind—
this fire is able to purify and eliminate them all.
The third is Māru, whose form and color are extremely black and parched;
he holds a cloth that flutters in the wind. This refers to the practitioner whose doubting mind repeatedly advances and retreats due to beginningless delusive confusion.
When the roots of affliction have not been severed, they constantly surround and bind one;
further obscured by darkness, one must repeatedly rely on this [wisdom] to incinerate them,
dispersing and destroying the heavy clouds.
The fourth is Raudra, whose physical form is perfectly proportioned;
he has a triple-peaked garland of blazing flames, his color is like the radiance of the rising sun,
and he holds a sword with a slightly wrathful expression.
The fifth is Mṛṇāla; his honored form is pale yellow.
Upon his body are beard, mustache, and hair; upon his crown is great majestic light.
His left eye is wrathful and his right is smiling; his left side is red and his right is yellow.
In the triangle to the left of the seat, Samaya holds a sword and Prajñā holds a vajra;
they are able to accomplish two kinds of deeds: summoning and pacifying.
The sixth is the wrathful fire deity, whose honored form and color are like flames.
Closing one eye and letting out a great roar, with dog-like teeth bared above and below,
and hair bristling upward on the head— these two matters are both fire and wind.
The seventh is named "Warming the Belly," which is the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Swift and extremely wrathful, the syllable HŪṂ possesses five colors.
The eighth is named Vikiraṇa; its color is like a mass of lightning, most difficult to behold. He sits within a vajra-maṇḍala.
Able to dispel heavy obscurations, As well as the retinue of the Summit Practice,
The ninth fire of the mind-born— This Honored One accomplishes according to one's will,
With various bodies through universal gates, Possessing great power and sovereign wisdom.
The tenth is named Kālavī; on the right side of that Honored One is the mudrā and sound of the "Oṃ" of Pure Conduct.
The eleventh is missing its name in the Sanskrit manuscript.
Twelve mu-ha-na: the venerable form amidst the kalpa-ending fires;
at the site of enlightenment, he subdues Māra.
Those who commit evil cannot be stopped; though exhorted and guided, they only increase further.
This fire can purify and remove [defilements]; through skillful means it subdues them, causing the deluded and ignorant mind to become subtle and secret, gradually leading one into the Way.
Next, one should set forth the four subtle mysteries; the ritual procedures should be practiced.
Through the mantras and mudrās of the *iṣṭadevatā*, body, speech, and mind are brought into correspondence.
When these three positions are perfectly harmonized, one performs all ritual activities.
Inducing from the external into the internal, the meaning and principle are without distinction.
The rite for pacifying (śāntika) begins at the first watch of the night; the rite for increasing (paustika) begins during the first division of the day.
One should perform fierce subjugation at midday;
summoning at all times;
and performing rites of love at night.
May there be intelligence and long life, as well as the methods for removing obstacles and difficulties;
may the oppressions of the five planets, all manner of calamities and misfortunes,
disputes and quarrels, and the pressures of the royal court be eliminated.
When those within and without are not in harmony, the seven luminaries deviate from their regular courses;
wind and rain do not come at their proper times, pestilence and famine arise,
and malevolent spirits and various portents of ill omen appear.
Facing north, sit with the thighs crossed; place the right thigh forward and keep the knees upright.
One's clothing should be pure white, and the ground for eating and drinking should be fragrant and adorned with flowers;
the same applies to the lamps and candles. Arrange the maṇḍala of the moon disk and inscribe the mantras upon it.
The written characters should also be white; dwelling in the contemplation of the three gates of liberation, one enters the samādhi of emptiness.
Moving the mind throughout the entire dharma-realm, suddenly there is not a single dharma to be found. In a mere moment, the mind becomes tranquil.
To eliminate all views, one removes attachment to emptiness;
Entering the samādhi of signlessness, one is freed from all signs;
Next, through the samādhi of wishlessness, regarding that wisdom of suchness,
Free from marks, fundamentally empty and still, there is likewise nothing to be wished for or sought.
Arising from samādhi, contemplate clearly within the breast:
the perfect luminosity, measuring about one cubit, is the bodhicitta, like the light of the autumn moon.
Transparency and clarity are held reverently in the heart.
The secret syllables he maintains clearly form the path of letters;
they enter the mouth of Yoga, arranged in a clockwise rotation of characters.
Arrayed within the moon-disc of the mind, each syllable is golden in color;
emitting great radiance, with body and mind undisturbed,
one enters the gateway of the letter "A," and thus, for each and every syllable,
Contemplating the meaning of the true nature (dharmatā) is called the mindfulness of samādhi.
First, recite the refuge formula together; after three times seven [recitations], remove it.
Beginning with "Oṃ," for the sake of removing calamities for such-and-such a person.
At the end of "svāhā," the *mūlamantra* is added according to the specific rite.
One should recite with a low voice, maintaining a tranquil mind while visualizing the wrathful form of the Protector.
The furnace is circular, though its shape may also be square; it measures one cubit in width and half a cubit in depth.
The base of the furnace is fashioned from clay into the form of a wheel, which possesses eight spokes.
Its height is one span, with each spoke being one finger-breadth thick, and its circumference consists of four sections.
The altar is smeared with pure white pigment, with other fragrances applied accordingly;
upon the steps, auspicious *śara* grass is spread, turning to the right with the passage of the sun, its tips covered by their bases.
Alternatively, various colors may be spread, radiating a brilliant crimson glow in extreme magnificence.
When all the painted images are completed, one should offer incense of agallochum,
ghee lamps, and various fresh, exquisite flowers and fruits, as well as food and drink, as offerings.
From the first day of the month until the eighth day, one should perform homa at the three remaining times of the day.
With a mind of loving-kindness, one gives rise to joy and gazes upon all beings;

this is the brief procedure for *homā*. One should employ the *vidyā* of Karmasādhana or Acala, and with the king of *vidyās*, Kilikilīya, perform the binding of protection (*rakṣā*) over the ritual objects.
The wisdom-feather presses down upon the earth, extending the remaining pāramitās;
one sprinkles everywhere with scented water. The mantra says:
"If you wish to perform all ritual activities and achieve the dharma of binding the maṇḍala,"
Protecting oneself and one’s disciples, and dispelling all obstacles and difficulties—
by virtue of this mudrā and mantra, the devaputras of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens shall constantly come to that place, observing and ensuring swift realization.
The hearth is set facing the maṇḍala; it is constructed separately from the outer perimeter.
The offerings are as prescribed for the great altar, and half of the hearth is filled with burning charcoal.
Branches produced from trees—such as milky wood and dry firewood—are used.
Cast [the fuel] into the midst of the maṇḍala; do not use old fire-sticks for the spark, and do not fan the flame with the mouth.
Immediately sprinkle pure scented water and light the brazier while reciting the following mantra:
Once the fire has emitted its radiant flames, the Wrathful King, free from defilement, empowers all things through the pervasive application of the mantra; every contact is thus called "mantra.
One should then visualize the syllable *ra*, which transforms into the Honored One of Fire.
Body crimson, hair yellow; three eyes and four arms, with flames blazing from every limb.
The wheel of space is bent into the palm, pressed down by earth, water, and fire.
The wind-song hook-call invokes:
"I now prostrate and entreat you, O Honored One, foremost among the Fire Heaven deities!
You who are revered by those practicing the Brahma-faring—may you deign to descend here."
"Accept this homa offering.
The mantra for the invitation is:

"Oṃ eheye mahābhūtanivāraṇi cihna-jaṣṭamā gṛhīta vahoḍima hāraṃ mā asmi saṃnihitobhava agnaye hayivakavibhavahānyai svāhā. The Fire Deity arrives and takes his seat; seal and sprinkle the fire with purification water.
Form small bundles of *kuśa* grass or the triple-pronged mudrā, and sprinkle water into the hearth with the mantra for purifying the fire:
"Oṃ amṛte hana hana hūṃ phaṭ. Scatter flowers upon Kuṇḍalī and offer *argha* perfumed water.
Extending the *vāyu* from the *vajramuṣṭi*, stir the *argha* water;
sprinkling it into the hearth by turning to the right, visualize it rinsing the mouth of the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*).
The mantra of auspiciousness is as follows:
The various components for the homa ritual are all prepared on the right side;
the two ladles and the empty vessel, along with the ghee, honey, oil, firewood, and so forth, are placed on the left.
One should perform the homa according to the prescribed rite.
With both hands placed upon the two knees, rotate them clockwise;
with the *dhairya-mudrā*, hold the *akṣamālā* and the *vajra-muṣṭi*; extend the *vāyu-mudrā* and the great *śrukā*;
let the small one be held by the wisdom hand; thus take up the *ghṛta* three times.
Filling the large ladle to the brim— wisdom abandons the small and grasps the great—
one pours it at the end of the verse onto the fire, casting it into the mouth of the Fire Deity:
oil and honey, milk and curd, rice porridge and porridge of the five grains.
With cooked rice and rice blossoms, one makes three successive offerings;
likewise with sweet fruits, plums, trees, roses, milk-trees and the like,
as well as aloeswood, sandalwood, cypress, maple, and oak, each measuring one span in length.
Either with ten fingers or four fingers, as thick as the index finger, with both ends smeared with ghee,
one casts them into the *muṇḍa* fire. [One may also offer] cloves, white sandalwood, aloeswood, frankincense,
camphor, cardamom, white mustard seeds, and *sahakāra* (stychia) resin.
Half powdered and half made into pills, the pills are mixed with ghee and honey;
as before, they are cast into the fire, three times in this manner.
Whether one hundred and eight times or twenty-one times, one then pours [the liquid] over the fire twenty-one times with a small ladle, reciting the mantra as follows:
Drawing out the sound of the syllable “Ha,” then suppressing it until it aligns with the fruit;
the practitioner stands to the left, while the Master, wielding the vajra with wisdom,
hooks the earth and the empty wheel to cause the Fire God to receive his food offering.
The mantra for the *śāntika* homa is as follows:

*Namo samanta-buddhānām | Ā mahā-śāntikara śāntikara prāsama-dharmanirjāta | Abhava svabhāva dharma-samata-prāpta svāhā.* [One] should request the Fire God (*Agnideva*) to emerge from the hearth and take his place in the southeast direction.
Next, holding an incense burner, one should request the planetary deities (*graha*) of their respective palaces.
As well as Āyuṣmat-karma and Garbha-nakṣatra, with the mudrās of the fist and the hook of wind and fire;
having made offerings, they return to their original positions.
With both hands holding seasonal flowers, they remove impurities and bring forth radiance.
Alternatively, the presiding master may perform the empowerment by casting [the flowers] across the hearth.
Visualize that the flowers pervade all the seats. Purify the fire once more as before, and invite the Honored One into the hearth.
Invite each one individually with their respective root mantra and present offerings; or, with a sincere heart, offer to the deities of the hall and their retinues together.
Vast clouds stream forth— food, banners, and parasols—
pervading lands as numerous as motes of dust;
wherever their light shines and touches, all sentient beings in the three evil realms [are relieved].
The suffering ceases and body and mind find joy;
having completed the three rounds of homa, all the offered incense, flowers,
and food are blended together as one.
Together with their retinues and hundreds of officials, all sentient beings throughout the dharma realm each protect themselves in three ways.
Finally, at the four sides of the hearth, there are various foods, drinks, and fruits.
One performs the empowerment through homa.
After the master has come out and washed his hands, he again, in a pure place, makes offerings to the deities of the eight directions.
Returning once more, he again makes offerings to the fire, as well as to the lunar mansions, planets, and so forth, three times each.
Rejoicing, he took leave of the devas:
"By the great power and sovereign majesty of the devas, The immeasurable vows of sentient beings can be fulfilled.
I prostrate to all the devas and return to my own palace; Should there be a time in the future when you sincerely entreat me with compassion,"
"I only pray that you will come here to receive this offering. The mantra says:
"If one seeks increase, it is called pauṣṭika."
Associated with a joyful mind, from the ninth to the fifteenth day of the month,
one attains the five supernormal powers and the treasure-store; together with the sword, wheel, vajra, wealth,
medicinal pills, and eye-salve, there is the advancement of honor and the increase of lifespan.
Merit, wisdom, and renown; official duties based on royal office;
auspiciousness, excellence, and peace; facing east in the full lotus posture, with garments all yellow;
increasing or decreasing the mantra syllables.
As before, there is no difference;
pervading the realms of the ten directions and illuminating all sentient beings,
they all attain prosperity and flourish, achieving wealth, honor, and long life.
This very cloud of light, at those places where they dwell,
rains down the requisites of the seven treasures and further rains down the nectar of heaven,
pouring into the hearts of those who practice.
Circular and with a depth of half a cubit, the base is fitted with a three-pronged vajra; its dimensions follow the previous standard.
For the deities Prabhāsvara and Bṛhaspati, as well as Śrīmitra, Manojava, and others, their mudrās are as previously described, and their offerings follow the preceding ritual protocol.
Named Baddhasikara, associated with a mind of joy and anger;
[recited] sixteen and twenty-three times, it summons humans,
devas, nāgas, spirits, and non-humans, who are all held in reverence and love.
May one's family, state, and kinsmen, as well as enemies and all friends, be harmonious and joyful; may one also seek sublime eloquence.
May the eight classes of beings—devas and nāgas—and all Buddhas and bodhisattvas likewise be so.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas protect and keep [the practitioner] in mind in all places.
For those whose sought-after vows are fulfilled, they sit with their faces turned westward in the half-lotus posture;
may their supreme aspirations increase accordingly, and may they gather [the merit] for such-and-such a person.
With a joyful mind, the Vidyādhara— whose protective deity manifests both peaceful and wrathful forms—
summons with the vajra hook and offers clouds of hooks to the Dharmadhātu.
Next, he summons those in the three lower realms and establishes them among humans and gods.
One shoots at the two vehicles’ weariness and renunciation, At hatred, resentment, and the three heavy obstacles,
And at the mind of malice and harm, Causing them to reach the Stage of Supreme Joy.
One shoots at five locations:
Open the flower-base and its filaments; measure one cubit in length and half a cubit in depth.
At the bottom, place a red lotus flower; the two-layered rim is four finger-widths wide.
Pressing against the empty space, raise the wind-wheel (the thumb); at each of the four sides, there is a single dot.
Thus the great boundary was established.
He lit lamps with fruit oil and made offerings of milk, thorny fruits, firewood, and red flowers.
With hair crimson and deep blue, you are the son of Brahmā, the Great White One.
To those who have entered the womb, their parents, and others, you grant universal protection and joy.
If one performs rites of subjugation, such as the *abhicāruka*, [you grant success].
When twenty-four months have passed, he shall subdue malevolent spirits and wicked men,
destroy the Eye of the True Dharma, and likewise the various evil venomous dragons that send untimely torrential rains and frost and hail to ruin the crops.
Floods and droughts occur out of season, and malevolent spirits spread everywhere;
strange portents appear in every place, and the masses find no peace.
Disorder and turmoil prevail wherever they go, as people fail to practice loyalty and filial piety.
This Dharma is able to subdue and eliminate [afflictions], for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the world;
thus it establishes this great skillful means to simultaneously benefit others.
Internally giving rise to a mind of compassion, externally it manifests great wrath.
Pressing the left big toe with the right, sit in a squatting posture facing south;
visualize all colors as dark blue-black, and contemplate a luminous orb within the heart that transforms into a great sun-disc, blazing with a brilliance beyond compare.
Radiant like the conflagration at the end of an eon, recite the mantra with fierce diligence;
while others may seem to listen, the Protector remains with a tranquil mind—
thus one should contemplate the Wrathful Lord!
Streaming forth clouds of ritual implements as offerings that fill all of space,
may all the wrathful deities rain down these implements upon those who dwell above.
Place a single-pronged pestle in the center, its dimensions equal to those of the Baddhaka;
smear the ground of the mandala with red and black pigments.
Sit upon a thorny tree seat strewn with red flowers and odorless black flowers, scattering them to serve as an offering.
Place a small amount each of black flowers, mustard seeds, and cypress in the argha;
for incense, use guggulu; use mustard oil as the wick and ox fat with rudhira as the lamp; thus make offerings to the Holy Honored One.
The Wrathful Universal Protection mantra is as follows:
Circumambulate Kuṇḍalī in succession and spread foul-smelling thorny grass.
Place *kuśa* root in the incense burner; when the fire is lit, sprinkle pure water.
The syllable “RAṂ” becomes the Fire Deity, crimson-black with pervasive smoke and flames.
Perform the invitation as before, using ox fat, *rudhira*, blood, clarified butter, milk, honey, and sesame oil.
Mix *viṣa* together with head-vinegar, or use it alone; cast *muṇḍa* [seeds] twenty-one times.
Using bone, hair, wood from evil trees, thorns, and *viṣa*, dip them in *rudhira-oil* and pour it everywhere while reciting the mantra.
Indicating the original direction, he makes this invocation to pacify the planet Mars (Huo):
"To the stars of the lunar mansions Shen (Śravaṇā) and Liu (Jyeṣṭhā), I make this vow and offer praise and hymns:
'O Great Deity of wrathful majestic power, You can fulfill the needs of sentient beings and destroy their enemies.'"
Now, seeking to defeat the enemy and extinguish our foes, we bow our heads to the various devas and return to our own palace.
Hereafter, when there is a time for sincere and compassionate entreaty, we pray only that you will descend to receive our offerings.
The mantra for the respectful dismissal is as follows:
Following the ritual procedures for dissolving the boundary, one stands directly before the Honored One;
stretching the limbs repeatedly, one spits full-mouthfuls and makes grunting sounds.
Regarding such matters as these, O Great Ācārya of the Mahāyāna! You must restrain yourself and not be arrogant.
If you wish to seek great siddhi, you ought to perform homa frequently.
Every time three lakṣas have been completed, perform a fire offering once.
Furthermore, as for the characteristics of the homa: the flames are red or golden, as glossy as cow’s ghee; the fragrance and the flames are without sound.
From the upper flames, heavy flames arise, dispersing into the shape of a parasol.
Within the objects empowered by this rite— whether warm smoke or radiant light—
a great sound issues forth, like the Brahma-voice or the lion’s roar.
The subtle resonance of thunder, the elegant sounds of bells and drums—
know these as signs of accomplishment.
His complexion is radiant and lustrous, and great stars emerge from it.
Or if there is a foul stench like smoke, one should know that the embers have arisen and entered the earth;
thus one should understand the internal and external obstructions.
Or if one dreams of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajradharas, or various kings, [one should likewise understand the signs].
The Lord of the Family, the Lord of Mantras, the Vidyārāja, or the Triple Gem;
O Brahmin or householder!
Clad in fresh, exquisite white garments and adorned with various necklaces and ornaments upon your body.
Beautiful women in exquisite attire, some pregnant or carrying infants,
holding vessels of incense, flowers, and canopies;
they walk along the path surrounding [him], eating non-glutinous rice and curd-rice.
Ambrosia, milk, fruit, and flowers; thick forests as if climbing a mountain;
treading upon stupas and multi-storied pavilions;
lions, oxen, and deer, white cranes, and the king of peacocks.
A garuḍa and a boat float upon the pure waters of the ocean;
or one soars freely through the air, with flames pervading the body,
seated within the Dharma seat for listening to the teachings.
Obtaining rare and wondrous jewels—conch shells, wheels, swords, and vajras;
being comforted with kind words; auspicious clouds together with flashes of lightning;
gentle breezes raining down celestial flowers; and the fragrance of incense as well as ritual ablutions.
All these are but accomplishments; having awakened, do not sleep again.
If in a dream one encounters executioners, or pigs, donkeys, camels, and dogs—whether they touch one or remain nearby—and likewise if one encounters corpses, [one should know this to be so].
Malevolent spirits and their fearful hordes, bodies clad in tattered rags,
women of hideous form, and all inauspicious things—
these are obstacles that prevent accomplishment.
Violating the samaya, one is bound within earth and water;

the wheel of fire encircles the two winds. By uniting the front [wheels] and practicing the great wheel, the obstacles of the twenty-one [stages] are all dissolved; the Mother of the Sleep Family provides protection.
The Lord of the Family protects one’s dwelling; Inauspicious and evil dreams [are dispelled] by reciting the Vidyārājñī mantra a hundred times.
The Vidyādhara honors the tutelary deity; [He recites] the mantra of the Vidyārāja of the Family.
Regarding the consecrated food and the food itself, the homa ritual, and the methods of veneration—
if one understands these only superficially and fails to accord even slightly with their requirements,
all manner of evils will gather there.
One shall always behold the Honored One, The mind penetrating the gates of liberation;
Wisdom is unfathomable, And all worldly and world-transcending aspirations are fulfilled.

This *Mandala-homa-vidhi* compiles the entirety of this ritual method; it is the essential path of [the syllables] A and VAṂ. It is a secret record brought back by Great Master Jikaku, which is not included in the *Ninniku*.

However, as it was transcribed through successive copies, many errors occurred. I have now collated what was missing and brought it to life through carving upon woodblocks; I hope that those among the wise who encounter this will correct whatever remains amiss.

At this time, in the year of the Yuanwen cycle, the *xiāngshè* (stellar mansion) of *Qiángyǔ Dàhuāngluò*, during the final month of summer, the heat and drought were extraordinary, as if one were inside a steamer. By day I lectured on the scriptures, and by night I engaged in the work of collation, doing so solely out of a diligent and earnest devotion to the Dharma.
At the base of the valley of Mount Hōon lies peerless consciousness.
